feedback: If a learner says 'the bulb makes the light': ask where the energy came from before the bulb lit \u2014 the bulb provides a pathway for energy from the battery to leave as light; it does not contain or create light from nothing.
If a learner asserts transfer without evidence: ask 'how do you know energy got there?' and steer them to the observable result (bulb lit, ear heard, thermometer/surface rose).

If a learner thinks transfer always needs touching: contrast the light/Sun case and radiated warmth crossing a gap with the hot-pan-to-spoon contact case \u2014 light and radiated heat cross a gap without touching.
If a learner says energy is 'used up on the way': reframe as energy transferred to the destination and its surroundings, not destroyed.

If a learner won't count sound or light as carrying energy ('they're just what you hear and see'): show light warming or illuminating a surface and a loud sound making something vibrate \u2014 they DO carry energy that can make something happen.

If a learner treats heat as a substance that 'leaks out' (the 'hotness' flows away): reframe heat as energy transferred from the hotter object to the cooler one because of the temperature difference \u2014 there is no 'heat stuff', just energy moving.
activities.intendedInsight: The same story \u2014 energy starts here, travels by some means, arrives there \u2014 holds across all four cases; energy is transferred from a source to a destination through a pathway, and you can evidence that it arrived.
learnerActions: Set up or observe each of four transfers and, for each, say out loud where the energy STARTS (source) and where it ENDS UP (destination): a buzzer/drum sends energy as sound to your ear; a lamp or the Sun sends energy as light across a gap to a surface; a hot object (e.g. a hot pan) warms a cooler one (e.g. a cold spoon) by contact; a battery sends energy along wires to a bulb.

For every case, answer 'How do you know the energy got there?' with the observed evidence \u2014 the bulb lit, the ear heard, the surface was lit up or warmed, the thermometer/spoon rose in temperature.
Before running each case, trace or draw an arrow from source to destination predicting the path the energy will take, then check it.
State for each case that energy moved from where it started to where it ended up, using the same 'source \u2192 pathway \u2192 destination' wording every time.
activities.title: Observe four transfers: source \u2192 pathway \u2192 destination

feedback: If a learner thinks the current is 'used up' in the bulb: clarify that it is ENERGY that is transferred at the bulb, not the charge \u2014 the charge circulates round the loop and returns to the battery.
If a learner says the bulb stores or makes the light: point back to the break-the-loop observation \u2014 no complete path, no arrival, no light.

If the loop won't light, check for a break in the pathway (loose or wrong connections, a blown bulb) and also check the battery is not flat: the loop must be complete, and the battery must still have energy to give, for the bulb to light.
activities.intendedInsight: A complete circuit provides a pathway for energy to travel from the battery to the bulb; the bulb shines only because energy reached it, not because it 'contains' light.
learnerActions: Join a battery to a bulb with wires to complete a loop and observe the bulb light; then break the loop and observe the bulb go out.
Say what the complete loop allows ('energy can reach the bulb') and what the break stops ('energy can't get there').

Describe the chain: the battery gives energy to the current, the current carries energy along the wires to the bulb, where it is transferred to light and heat (an old-style filament bulb gives off much more heat than light).
Optionally, trace the energy arrow from battery to bulb before completing the circuit, then run it to check.
activities.title: Make and break the electric pathway
